topics.title: The medieval Church and the Crusades
topics.intro: In medieval Europe almost everyone was Christian, and the Church shaped every part of life, from birth to death. In 1095 the Pope called on Christians to fight for Jerusalem.
topics.teach: Explain why the Church was so powerful in medieval England.
topics.talk: Ask her why ordinary people went on pilgrimages.

topics.title: Henry II and Thomas Becket
topics.intro: Henry II made his friend Thomas Becket Archbishop of Canterbury, expecting him to do as he was told. It ended in murder in a cathedral.
topics.teach: Explain why Henry II and Becket fell out.
topics.talk: Ask her who was more to blame for Becket’s murder: Henry or Becket himself?

topics.title: King John and Magna Carta
topics.intro: King John lost wars, quarrelled with the Pope and taxed his barons heavily. In 1215 they forced him to agree to a charter: Magna Carta.
topics.teach: Explain why Magna Carta still matters today.
topics.talk: Ask her what “nobody is above the law” has to do with 1215.

topics.title: Life in a medieval village
topics.intro: Most people in medieval England were peasants who lived in villages, farmed strips of land and owed work to their lord.
topics.teach: Describe a day in the life of a medieval peasant.
topics.talk: Ask her what a villein had to do for the lord of the manor.

topics.title: The Black Death
topics.intro: In 1348 a terrible disease reached England. Within two years it had killed between a third and a half of the population.
topics.teach: Explain what people at the time thought caused the Black Death, and what really caused it.
topics.talk: Ask her how the Black Death made life better for some peasants who survived.

topics.title: The Peasants’ Revolt, 1381
topics.intro: In 1381 thousands of peasants marched on London, captured the Tower and met the 14-year-old king. Why did they rebel?
topics.teach: Explain the difference between a long-term cause and a trigger, using the Peasants’ Revolt.
topics.talk: Ask her what the poll tax was and why it made people so angry.

topics.title: The Hundred Years War and the Wars of the Roses
topics.intro: For over a century English kings fought to rule France. Then the great families of England fought each other for the crown.
topics.teach: Explain how the Wars of the Roses ended and who became king.
topics.talk: Ask her what the Tudor rose stands for.

topics.title: The Tudors: Henry VIII to Elizabeth I
topics.intro: Henry VIII broke with the Pope so he could remarry. His three children each changed England’s religion again. Was Elizabeth’s reign a “golden age”?
topics.teach: Explain why Henry VIII broke with the Church in Rome.
topics.talk: Ask her the order of Henry VIII’s six wives, using “divorced, beheaded, died…”.

items.prompt: Who was the head of the Church across western Europe in the Middle Ages?
items.explain: The Pope, in Rome, led the Catholic Church across western Europe.

items.prompt: What was the tax of one tenth of everything a peasant produced, paid to the Church?
items.explain: Peasants paid a tithe (one tenth) of their crops and animals to the Church.

items.prompt: Where did medieval Christians believe souls went to be cleansed of sins before Heaven?
items.explain: Fear of Purgatory made people pray, give money and go on pilgrimages to shorten their time there.

items.prompt: What is a journey to a holy place called?
items.explain: Pilgrims travelled to shrines such as Canterbury, Rome, Santiago de Compostela or Jerusalem.

items.prompt: Men who lived in a monastery, following a strict rule of prayer and work, were called…
items.explain: Monks (and nuns, in nunneries) prayed, copied books by hand and cared for the sick and poor.

items.prompt: Which Pope called the First Crusade in 1095?
items.explain: At Clermont in 1095, Pope Urban II urged knights to recapture Jerusalem, promising forgiveness of their sins.

items.prompt: In which year did the First Crusaders capture Jerusalem?
items.explain: The crusaders took Jerusalem in 1099 and killed many of its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants.

items.prompt: Which Muslim leader recaptured Jerusalem in 1187?
items.explain: Saladin, Sultan of Egypt and Syria, defeated the crusaders at Hattin and took Jerusalem in 1187. He was respected even by his enemies.

items.prompt: Which English king led the Third Crusade (1189–92)?
items.explain: Richard I, “the Lionheart”, won battles but never recaptured Jerusalem. He spent only about six months of his reign in England.

items.prompt: Why did many knights join the First Crusade?

options.text: A mix of faith, forgiveness and hope of land
Only because the king forced them to go
options.feedback: Kings did not force most crusaders. Many went because of their faith and the Pope’s promise.

options.text: To spread the English language and laws
options.feedback: Crusaders came from all over western Europe; language had nothing to do with it.

items.explain: Historians stress mixed motives: genuine faith, the Pope’s promise of forgiveness, adventure, and for some, land and wealth.

items.prompt: In which year did Henry II become king?
items.explain: Henry II ruled from 1154 to 1189, over England and much of France (the Angevin Empire).

items.prompt: Which job did Henry II give Thomas Becket in 1162?
items.explain: Henry expected his friend and chancellor to support him as head of the English Church. Instead Becket defended the Church against the king.

items.prompt: What did Henry and Becket quarrel about most?
items.answer: which courts should try criminal priests
distractors: who should marry Henry’s eldest daughter
where to build a great new cathedral
whether England should join a crusade
items.explain: Church courts gave lighter punishments. Henry wanted “criminous clerks” punished in royal courts (Constitutions of Clarendon, 1164).

items.prompt: In which year was Thomas Becket murdered in Canterbury Cathedral?
items.explain: Four knights killed Becket on 29 December 1170 after Henry reportedly raged against him.

items.prompt: What happened to Becket’s reputation after his murder?
distractors: his tomb was destroyed at once
items.explain: Becket was made a saint in 1173. Henry did public penance at his tomb in 1174. Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales are about pilgrims going to his shrine.

items.prompt: Edward Grim, a monk who was injured trying to protect Becket, wrote an account of the murder. What makes it especially useful to historians?

options.text: He was an eyewitness who was there in the cathedral
He was the king’s official historian
options.feedback: He was a monk, not working for the king.

options.text: It was written hundreds of years later with more information
options.feedback: He wrote soon after the event, which is part of its value.

items.explain: Eyewitness accounts give vivid detail, though historians remember Grim admired Becket, which may shape how he told the story.

items.prompt: Which king agreed to Magna Carta?
items.explain: King John (ruled 1199–1216) agreed to Magna Carta in 1215.

items.prompt: Where was Magna Carta agreed in 1215?
items.explain: John met the rebel barons in a meadow at Runnymede, by the Thames near Windsor, in June 1215.

items.prompt: Which group forced John to agree to Magna Carta?
items.explain: Rebel barons, angry at heavy taxes and failed wars, captured London and forced John to negotiate.

items.prompt: Which part of France did King John lose in 1204, earning him the nickname “Softsword”?
items.explain: Losing Normandy, the homeland of the Norman kings, was a huge blow to John’s reputation.

items.prompt: Magna Carta said no free man could be imprisoned except by “the lawful judgement of his equals or by the law of the land”. Why does this matter today?

options.text: It says even the ruler must obey the law
It gave every adult the right to vote
options.feedback: Voting rights came centuries later.

options.text: It freed all the peasants from their lords
options.feedback: It protected “free men”, mainly barons. Most peasants were not free.

items.explain: Magna Carta mostly protected the barons, but its idea that the king is under the law inspired later rights, including the US Constitution.

items.prompt: In 1265, whose parliament first included ordinary townsmen (burgesses) as well as nobles?
items.explain: Simon de Montfort, rebelling against Henry III, called a parliament with knights and burgesses: an important step towards today’s Parliament.

items.prompt: The land and village owned by a lord was called a…
items.explain: A manor included the lord’s house, his land (the demesne) and the villagers’ strips.

items.prompt: What was a peasant called who was not free and had to work on the lord’s land?
items.explain: Villeins (serfs) could not leave the manor without permission and owed the lord several days’ work a week.

items.prompt: How was farmland usually divided in a medieval village?
items.answer: into strips in large open fields
distractors: into equal squares for each family
it was not divided at all
items.explain: Each family farmed scattered strips in two or three huge open fields, with one field left fallow (resting) each year.

items.prompt: Which villager made sure everyone did their work for the lord?
items.explain: The reeve was a peasant chosen to organise work on the lord’s land.

items.prompt: What was medieval England’s most valuable export?
items.explain: English wool was sold across Europe. The Lord Speaker still sits on a “Woolsack” in the House of Lords.

items.prompt: What was the main food of medieval peasants?
items.explain: Peasants ate bread, pottage and ale. Potatoes did not arrive in Europe until after 1500.

items.prompt: What do scientists now know caused the Black Death?

options.text: A bacterium spread by fleas
Bad smells, or “miasma”, in the air
options.feedback: Many people at the time believed in “miasma”, but smells don’t cause plague.

options.text: An unlucky line-up of the planets
options.feedback: Medieval doctors blamed the planets, but it was a bacterium.

options.text: God punishing people for their sins
options.feedback: This was a common belief at the time, but the cause was a disease.

items.explain: The plague bacterium (Yersinia pestis) was spread by flea bites, and the pneumonic form passed from person to person through coughing.

items.prompt: In which year did the Black Death reach England?
items.explain: It arrived at Melcombe (now part of Weymouth) in Dorset in 1348.

items.prompt: Roughly how much of England’s population died in the Black Death?
items.explain: Historians estimate 30 to 50% of the population died in 1348–50.

items.prompt: What were people called who whipped themselves in public, hoping God would end the plague?
items.explain: Flagellants believed that punishing themselves might win God’s forgiveness.

items.prompt: Many medieval people believed disease was spread by “bad air”. What was this idea called?
items.explain: Miasma theory lasted until germ theory in the 1860s. People carried sweet-smelling herbs to protect themselves.

items.prompt: Why did wages rise after the Black Death?

options.text: Workers were scarce, so they could demand more
The king ordered higher wages to help peasants
options.feedback: In fact the government tried to stop wages rising, with the Statute of Labourers (1351).

options.text: Lords became kinder and more generous after the plague
options.feedback: Lords paid more because they had to, not out of kindness.

items.explain: A labour shortage gave peasants bargaining power. The Statute of Labourers (1351) tried to cap wages, which caused deep resentment.

items.prompt: Which 1351 law tried to stop peasants demanding higher wages?
items.explain: The Statute of Labourers fixed wages at pre-plague levels: a long-term cause of the Peasants’ Revolt.

items.prompt: In which year was the Peasants’ Revolt?
items.explain: The revolt began in Essex and Kent in May and June 1381.

items.prompt: Which tax, charged on every adult, triggered the revolt?
items.explain: A third poll tax in 1380 charged everyone the same, rich or poor. Tax collectors in Essex were attacked in 1381.

items.prompt: Who led the rebels from Kent?
items.explain: Wat Tyler led the rebels into London. He was killed at Smithfield by the Lord Mayor, William Walworth.

items.prompt: Which preacher asked, “When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?”
items.explain: John Ball preached that God made everyone equal, so no one should be a serf.

items.prompt: How old was King Richard II when he met the rebels?
items.explain: Richard II was only 14. He met the rebels at Mile End and Smithfield.

items.prompt: Which of these was the TRIGGER of the Peasants’ Revolt (the spark), rather than a long-term cause?

options.text: Poll tax collectors arriving in Essex in 1381
Villeins working for their lords for centuries
options.feedback: This is a long-term cause: it had built up resentment over many years.

options.text: The Statute of Labourers, passed in 1351
options.feedback: This is a long-term cause, 30 years earlier.

options.text: John Ball’s long preaching about equality
options.feedback: Ball had preached for years. His ideas were a long-term cause.

items.explain: Long-term causes build up pressure; a trigger is the event that sets it off.

items.prompt: Historians disagree about the MAIN cause of the revolt. Which is the strongest argument?

options.text: Anger at serfdom: peasants wanted freedom, and the poll tax was just the last straw
options.feedback: Strong: the rebels’ demands at Mile End were mainly about ending serfdom, not just the tax.

options.text: The poll tax: it was unfair and had already been charged three times
options.feedback: A good argument, but the demands went much further than the tax, which suggests deeper causes.

options.text: Richard II was a weak king
options.feedback: The king’s youth mattered, but the rebels said they were loyal to him and blamed his advisers.

options.text: Bad weather that summer
options.feedback: There is no evidence weather caused the revolt.

items.explain: Strong history answers weigh causes. The rebels’ demands (an end to serfdom, cheap land rent) show what they really wanted.

items.prompt: What happened after the rebels went home?
distractors: Wat Tyler became the king’s adviser
the poll tax was doubled again
items.explain: Richard’s promises were cancelled and John Ball was executed. But in the long run lords found it harder to control peasants, and serfdom faded away over the next century.

items.prompt: The Hundred Years War actually lasted from 1337 until…
items.explain: It lasted 116 years, on and off.

items.prompt: Which weapon helped the English win at Crécy (1346) and Agincourt?
items.explain: English and Welsh archers could shoot about 10 arrows a minute.

items.prompt: Which king won the Battle of Agincourt in 1415?
items.explain: Henry V’s smaller, exhausted army defeated the French on 25 October 1415.

items.prompt: Which teenage French girl led an army to relieve the siege of Orléans in 1429?
items.explain: Joan said she heard voices from God. She was captured, tried by the English and burned at Rouen in 1431.

items.prompt: Which was the only part of France still held by England when the war ended in 1453?
items.explain: England kept Calais until 1558.

items.prompt: The Wars of the Roses were fought between which two families?
items.explain: The House of Lancaster (red rose) fought the House of York (white rose) from 1455 to 1487.

items.prompt: Which king is suspected of having his nephews, the “Princes in the Tower”, killed?
items.explain: The boys disappeared in 1483 after their uncle Richard took the throne. Historians still argue about what happened.

items.prompt: Who won the Battle of Bosworth in 1485 and became the first Tudor king?
items.explain: Richard III was killed at Bosworth. His skeleton was found under a Leicester car park in 2012.

items.prompt: What did the Tudor rose (red and white together) symbolise?
items.answer: the joining of Lancaster and York
distractors: the union of England and Scotland
items.explain: Henry VII (Lancaster) married Elizabeth of York in 1486, uniting the two families.

items.prompt: How many times did Henry VIII marry?
items.explain: Divorced, beheaded, died; divorced, beheaded, survived.

items.prompt: Put Henry VIII’s wives in order.
items.explain: “Divorced, beheaded, died; divorced, beheaded, survived.”

items.prompt: Why did Henry VIII break with the Catholic Church in Rome?

options.text: The Pope would not annul his first marriage
He had become a Protestant after reading Luther
options.feedback: Henry had actually written against Luther and was called “Defender of the Faith” by the Pope.

options.text: The Pope threatened to invade England
options.feedback: There was no papal invasion.

items.explain: Henry needed a male heir. When the Pope refused an annulment, Henry made himself head of the English Church (Act of Supremacy, 1534). Money and power mattered too.

items.prompt: Which 1534 law made Henry VIII Supreme Head of the Church of England?
items.explain: The Act of Supremacy (1534) cut England off from the Pope’s authority.

items.prompt: Between 1536 and 1541 Henry closed every monastery in England and took their wealth. What is this called?
distractors: the Enclosure of the Common Lands
items.explain: Henry gained huge wealth. The ruins of abbeys such as Fountains and Tintern date from this time.

items.prompt: Which of Henry VIII’s children became king in 1547, aged 9?
items.explain: Edward VI, son of Jane Seymour, made England more Protestant but died aged 15 in 1553.

items.prompt: Which Tudor queen tried to bring back Catholicism and had about 280 Protestants burned?
items.explain: Mary I (1553–58) was later nicknamed “Bloody Mary” by Protestant writers.

items.prompt: Elizabeth I reigned from 1558 until which year?
items.explain: Elizabeth reigned for 44 years and never married. The crown passed to James VI of Scotland.

items.prompt: In 1588 which country sent a huge fleet, the Armada, to invade England?
items.explain: Philip II of Spain’s Armada was scattered by English fire ships and storms.

items.prompt: Which Elizabethan sailor sailed all the way around the world (1577–80)?
items.explain: Drake was the first Englishman to circumnavigate the globe. To the Spanish he was a pirate.

items.prompt: Why do historians disagree about whether Elizabeth’s reign was a “golden age”?

options.text: It was glorious for some groups but hard for others
Some historians have not read the evidence
options.feedback: Historians disagree because they ask different questions and look at different evidence.

options.text: Nobody wrote anything down in Elizabeth’s time
options.feedback: There is lots of evidence from Elizabeth’s reign.

items.explain: Interpretations depend on whose experience you focus on and what you count as success. That is why a good answer weighs both sides.

items.prompt: Put these Tudor monarchs in order.
items.explain: Five Tudor monarchs ruled from 1485 to 1603.
